arXiv:2609.39207v2 [cs.RO] 12 Oct 2026

ASENA: Self-evolving Agents for Embodied Navigation

An-Chieh Cheng Affiliation: NVIDIA    Isabella Liu Affiliation: NVIDIA    Edmund Bu Affiliation: University of California, San Diego    Johan Bjorck Affiliation: NVIDIA    Hongxu Yin Affiliation: NVIDIA    Zhengyi Luo Affiliation: NVIDIA    Jan Kautz Affiliation: NVIDIA    Linxi “Jim” Fan Affiliation: NVIDIA    Yuke Zhu Affiliation: NVIDIA Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin    Sifei Liu Affiliation: NVIDIA
Abstract

We present ASENA, an embodied agent system that enables general-purpose coding agents to program humanoid navigation, manipulation, and interaction. Through a unified robot harness, agents read sensor data, write and execute programs, inspect recorded outcomes, repair failures, and reuse notes and executable skills while keeping their model weights fixed. We also introduce ASENA-VLN, a 4B monocular navigation policy that serves as an optional tool within this programmable system. ASENA-VLN predicts body-frame trajectories for both extended routes and short-horizon behaviors. Its shared vision-language decoder is trained on route instructions, visual question answering, and a newly curated dataset of geometry-derived atomic navigation tasks. As a standalone policy, ASENA-VLN achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 68.7% on R2R and 70.2% on RxR. When integrated with a coding agent, learned navigation improves ASENA’s success rate by 11 percentage points on both agentic benchmarks and reduces execution time. Persistent workspace evolution uses simulator feedback to improve success over ten passes through recurring 100-task subsets. Success increases from 72% to 98% on R2R and from 65% to 89% on RxR. On embodied question answering, ASENA achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with fewer interaction steps. On a Unitree G1, we demonstrate search, visual inspection, spatial reasoning, synthesized gestures, and mobile manipulation combining object pickup, carrying, and handoff without a pre-built map. These demonstrations illustrate how online programming extends robot behavior beyond route following and predefined skills.

Abstract

\absfont\theabstract

1 Introduction

A useful humanoid robot must do more than reach a destination. If asked to check whether a vending machine contains an item and return with an answer, it must decide where to search, recognize the item, remember the user’s location, and communicate what it found. Retrieving an object from a room also requires planning a grasp, picking it up, carrying it back, and handing it to the user. Navigation is therefore only one part of a larger task whose next step depends on what the robot observes.

A learned navigation policy provides movement capabilities, but such requests also require deciding what to inspect, how to act on objects, and what to communicate. These procedures depend on new observations and may extend beyond predefined skills. Coding agents can construct and revise them during a mission through programmatic access to sensing, computation, simulation, and action. Physical deployment also requires feedback tied to outcomes and a persistent workspace for retaining useful procedures.

We present ASENA, an embodied agent system that gives coding agents programmatic control of humanoid tasks through a unified robot harness (Fig. ASENA: Self-evolving Agents for Embodied Navigation). The agent can read sensors, derive geometry, inspect visualizations, and write programs that combine navigation, grasp planning, whole-body motion, and user interaction. Linked execution records let the agent inspect outcomes and revise these programs. A persistent workspace stores notes and executable skills. The system can improve through program revision while keeping its model weights fixed.

Learned policies can further expand this programmable toolset when suitable training data are available. Delegating motion to a specialized policy reduces repeated agent decisions and supports navigation behaviors that are difficult to specify geometrically. We develop ASENA-VLN, a 4B monocular navigation policy trained on route instructions and geometry-derived navigation atoms. Building on vision-and-language navigation (VLN) [2; 20; 55; 8; 42], ASENA-VLN predicts body-frame trajectories for both extended routes and short-horizon goals, such as approaching an object or passing through a doorway. We curate a new atomic navigation dataset that directly supervises these reusable, fine-grained behaviors and complements conventional route-level training. The policy remains an optional tool: a program may call it directly, combine it with geometric navigation, or complete a task using other available operations.

We make three contributions. First, we introduce a robot harness that lets coding agents program humanoid navigation, manipulation, and interaction while retaining executable skills and experience. Second, we develop a state-of-the-art monocular navigation policy that supports both route following and reusable atomic skills. Third, we show through evaluation that workspace evolution improves task performance while model weights remain fixed. We evaluate navigation and embodied question answering (EQA) in simulation and demonstrate navigation, mobile manipulation, and user interaction on a real-world Unitree G1 robot operating without a pre-built map.

2 Related Work

Code as policies

Code as Policies [22] composes perception and control APIs in programs. CaP-X [13] provides CaP-Gym and benchmarks how API abstraction and execution feedback affect coding agents for manipulation. ASPIRE [25] uses multimodal execution traces to diagnose failures, repair robot programs, and retain reusable skills.

Agentic self-improvement

Voyager [37] retains and repairs executable skills. Reflexion [36] retains textual feedback without weight updates. ENPIRE [43] couples real-robot reset and verification with agent-driven program synthesis and policy training. ASENA studies how a persistent workspace can evolve around a pretrained navigation policy while all model weights remain fixed. We quantify this workspace evolution in simulation and demonstrate the system’s capabilities on a physical robot.

Language-guided navigation

Topological approaches such as DUET and ETPNav [7; 1] address visual instruction following. Video-to-action policies such as NaVid, NaVILA, and StreamVLN [55; 8; 42] address the same task. LM-Nav [35] composes pretrained models. InstructNav [24] combines zero-shot reasoning with generic motion primitives. DualVLN and Qwen-RobotNav [41; 30] integrate high-level reasoning with learned navigation policies. Uni-LaViRA [11] studies unified language-vision-action translation. Our VLN policy is most closely related to video-to-action navigation policies. We focus on a lightweight 4B model with fine-grained atomic capabilities that coding agents can compose with other tools and retained programs. We evaluate both its standalone navigation performance and its utility within the full embodied agent system.

Embodied question answering

Explore-EQA [33] studies active exploration until an agent can answer with sufficient confidence. 3D-Mem and GraphEQA [45; 34] organize observations into spatial memories. MemoryEQA [51] extends the setting to longer-horizon, multi-target questions. FAST-EQA [52] focuses on efficient evidence gathering. We use these EQA settings to evaluate ASENA’s ability to compose perception, navigation, and memory tools. We also evaluate its ability to improve by revising persistent notes and executable skills while keeping model weights fixed.

3 Method

ASENA gives a coding agent programmatic access to a physical robot (Fig. 2). It brings sensing, computation, visualization, simulation, and action into a unified workflow for writing, running, and inspecting programs. The system records each run for later inspection, repair, and reuse. The agent can also invoke a learned navigation policy as an optional tool within the same interface.

3.1 Grounding Programs in Robot Feedback

On G1, ASENA exposes a 360-degree camera, LiDAR, odometry, a body IMU, and joint states, with a calibrated head RGB/stereo camera for manipulation. The coding agent processes and visualizes these inputs to estimate geometry, inspect objects, and monitor execution. When an action differs from its intent, the agent can inspect the recorded evidence and revise its program.

Navigation

The agent can plan motion with geometric tools or invoke ASENA-VLN for language-conditioned navigation. Geometric tools use LiDAR-based occupancy maps to plan waypoints and check obstacle clearance. ASENA-VLN predicts bounded body-frame trajectories from language and recent monocular observations (Sec. 3.3). The agent chooses when to invoke each tool, checks progress through new observations, and revises the plan as needed.

Manipulation

SAM 2 [32] object masks and depth measurements ground candidate grasps. The system can supplement geometric proposals with learned candidates from GraspGenX [15] when additional grasp options are needed. Inverse kinematics and motion planning convert these candidates into trajectories for reaching, lifting, and carrying. Before execution, the system rebuilds arm trajectories from measured joint states and checks joint limits, sampled self-collisions, and scene clearance. These checks include held-object clearance during lift and retraction. A separate controller opens and closes the optional YAM parallel grippers and reports jaw width and controller state. The agent can compose these tools with navigation to program object pickup and handoff.

Skill composition and execution

ASENA exposes sensing, control, and safety operations as callable atomic skills. The coding agent combines navigation, grasp planning, arm trajectories, and gripper commands with computation and interaction logic to create reusable task programs. It writes and revises task logic and motion plans using execution feedback, while physical execution interfaces remain fixed. The SONIC whole-body controller [26] executes body motion. Gripper commands use the separate YAM controller, and speech uses the onboard speaker.

Execution checks

ASENA validates generated gestures online in MuJoCo for pose continuity, joint and motion limits, and sampled self-collision. Failed validation returns the violated constraint to the agent for repair. Physical motion requires validation and operator approval, including motion requested by revised programs. An independent navigation safeguard enforces motion limits and rejects commands when odometry is stale or the battery level is low. Heartbeat-triggered stops and manual emergency halts provide additional protection.

3.2 Turning Execution into Retained Experience

ASENA records runs in MCAP format [12]. These records align sensor and robot states with actions, feedback, code, and visualizations. Replaying this evidence lets the agent identify where execution diverged from its intent and repair the responsible program.

After repairing a failure, ASENA can retain the solution for future tasks. We represent the workspace at revision kk as Wk=(Nk,Sk)W_{k}=(N_{k},S_{k}), where NkN_{k} contains notes and SkS_{k} contains executable skills. A fixed coding model consults this workspace while solving tasks. Between revisions, a separate fixed-weight improver uses execution traces 𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k} and feedback fkf_{k} to update the workspace:

Wk+1=Iϕ​(Wk,𝒯k,fk).W_{k+1}=I_{\phi}(W_{k},\mathcal{T}_{k},f_{k}). (1)

Model and controller weights remain fixed. In simulation, private workers may edit workspaces between passes, while writes are disabled during frozen evaluation. On G1, execution records and optional operator feedback support skill revision while robot motion is disabled.

3.3 Learning a Reusable Visual Navigation Policy

ASENA-VLN reduces repeated agent reasoning on challenging routes. This optional tool predicts bounded body-frame trajectories from language and recent monocular observations. The coding agent decides when to invoke it, checks progress, and combines it with other tools. Policy training expands navigation capabilities within the same programming interface.

Policy inputs

We extend a lightweight Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct [3] with dedicated token vocabularies for trajectories and pixel goals (Fig. 3). The model takes up to eight front-view frames and a structured JSON instruction. This interface makes the policy easy to invoke as a callable tool. The instruction specifies a concise navigation command and can optionally include a desired end pose, anchor objects, or motion constraints. Recency-weighted visual tokens preserve temporal context while emphasizing the latest observation.

Output representations

A shared autoregressive decoder predicts up to eight cumulative body-frame waypoints, each represented as (x,y,θ)(x,y,\theta). Fixed bins along each axis convert trajectory tokens into explicit motion targets without requiring a separate continuous action head. Pixel-goal tokens provide auxiliary supervision by encouraging the model to localize its intended destination in the image. Visual question answering retains the model’s original text vocabulary. A pixel goal is not directly executable and requires an additional motion planner or, in simulation, a shortest-path follower. All evaluations in this paper therefore use trajectory-token predictions rather than pixel goals.

Curated atomic-navigation data

A callable navigation policy must follow both extended routes and precise local commands. We therefore curate nine atomic navigation tasks in MP3D and HM3D. They cover behaviors such as moving a specified distance, rotating to a target heading, approaching an object from a given direction, aligning with a target, entering a room, passing through a doorway, following a corridor, and moving between floors. We generate and validate each task using geodesic distance, visibility, and scene geometry so that every instruction describes a feasible and measurable motion. Each instruction is paired with a waypoint trajectory and auxiliary pixel-goal supervision. These data directly teach the reusable, fine-grained operations that task programs can invoke and compose.

Training mixture

We train ASENA-VLN on a mixture of these atomic tasks, short-horizon ObjectNav, and vision-language-navigation data from R2R, RxR, ScaleVLN, and SRDF [2; 20; 40; 39]. We also include multi-view VQA data [4] to strengthen the model’s spatial understanding. To match our callable policy interface, we use GPT-5.5 [28] to re-caption the original navigation instructions into our structured JSON format. The re-captioned instructions include concise navigation commands and, when applicable, end poses, anchor objects, and motion constraints. The reported checkpoint uses fewer than 10K optimizer steps and fewer than 5M training samples, including repeats. Training uses a 3:1 mixture of trajectory prediction and spatial VQA.

4 Evaluation and Applications

We first evaluate ASENA-VLN as a standalone instruction-following policy and then evaluate the full ASENA system on object-goal navigation. We next study how the learned policy and retained workspace experience affect coding-agent performance with model weights fixed. Finally, we evaluate embodied question answering in simulation and demonstrate the system on a Unitree G1 robot.

4.1 Standalone VLN Policy

Table 1 evaluates ASENA-VLN independently of coding-agent planning on R2R’s shorter instructions and RxR’s longer, more detailed routes. We use 0.25 m forward steps and 15-degree rotations. Navigation error (NE) is the final goal distance in meters. Oracle success rate (OSR) measures entering the goal region, while success rate (SR) requires stopping there. SPL accounts for path efficiency and nDTW for reference-route similarity. All four are percentages. SPF denotes the simulator shortest-path follower used by pixel-goal methods.

4.2 Object-Goal Navigation

Table 2 evaluates search for an object that may not initially be visible. ASENA-VLN is trained primarily for atomic navigation behaviors rather than global exploration. We pair it with a separate VLM [14] that plans where to search and updates the plan from new observations.

On HM3D-v2 and HM3D-OVON, this combination of global search reasoning and learned local navigation achieves state-of-the-art results compared with published methods from [30; 61]. Performance remains consistent across seen, synonymous, and unseen OVON object categories, indicating that the system can handle variations in both object descriptions and the routes required to find them.

4.3 Complementary Agent and Policy Capabilities

Table 3 studies how coding agents and ASENA-VLN contribute to navigation performance. We compare published zero-shot methods, standalone ASENA-VLN, and ASENA instantiated with two coding backends. Our R2R and RxR Agentic Splits each contain 100 tasks, following the reduced-set evaluation practice of Uni-LaViRA and Open-Nav [11; 29]. All policy and agent variants use the same task IDs across ten scenes in each benchmark. Four RxR episodes produce non-finite NE or SPL values. We count them as failures for SR and compute NE and SPL over the remaining 96 episodes. Each coding agent starts with a fresh workspace. Claude Sonnet 5 runs at high effort, while GPT-6 Astra runs at maximum effort.

Strong coding agents navigate effectively without a learned policy

Using only geometric and programmatic tools, GPT-6 Astra achieves state-of-the-art performance and surpasses standalone ASENA-VLN. On R2R, its success rate also approaches the reported human performance of 90% SR. Its strong reasoning allows it to interpret instructions, construct routes, monitor progress, and recover from errors without relying on a learned navigation policy. These results establish coding agents themselves as strong zero-shot navigation systems.

Learned navigation improves weaker coding backends

The benefit of ASENA-VLN is more pronounced for Claude Sonnet 5. Adding the policy improves both success and path efficiency, increasing SR by 11 percentage points on both R2R and RxR. The specialized policy therefore compensates for limitations in route execution and enables a weaker coding backend to complete more tasks. In comparison, GPT-6 Astra already performs strongly without the policy and benefits less from it. On RxR, enabling the policy slightly reduces its success rate. The value of learned navigation therefore depends on the coding backend and how effectively it incorporates policy predictions into its plans.

Learned navigation reduces repeated agent interaction

A single ASENA-VLN call executes several motion decisions, reducing repeated observation and action requests. Mean tool calls fall for every backend and benchmark (Table 3): by 46.9%/51.0% on R2R/RxR for GPT-6 Astra and 59.2%/62.5% for Claude Sonnet 5. The policy therefore absorbs low-level navigation even when success changes little. These call reductions show that learned navigation can reduce agent interaction while improving less capable backends, complementing strong agents’ direct programmatic control.

4.4 Retained Experience Improves Recurring Tasks

We evaluate workspace evolution by repeatedly presenting the same tasks, scenes, instructions, and initial poses. In each pass, sixteen Claude Sonnet 5 workers at high effort execute the tasks and may retain programs, notes, and prior action sequences in private workspaces. Between passes, an improver uses their traces and feedback to update the canonical workspace. We run campaigns with and without ASENA-VLN on R2R and RxR using ground-truth feedback, while keeping all model, policy, and controller weights fixed.

As shown in Fig. 4, success improves across all four campaigns. Logged worker and improver costs decrease as the workspace evolves. These results show that retained experience can improve recurring-task performance and reduce cost without updating model weights.

The variants with and without ASENA-VLN reach similar final success rates on R2R, while the policy retains a clearer advantage on the longer RxR instructions. Tool-equipped workspaces also maintain higher SPL on both benchmarks, showing that ASENA-VLN improves path efficiency even when final success rates converge.

4.5 Embodied Question Answering

Embodied question answering (EQA) requires an agent to explore an environment, gather relevant visual evidence, and answer a question using as little motion as possible. We evaluate ASENA on HM-EQA and MT-HM3D using their released initial poses [33; 51]. Following the Explore-EQA teleportation protocol, each episode has a nominal step budget of 3​A3\sqrt{A} for a scene of area AA. We report answer accuracy and normalized exploration steps, defined as the fraction of this nominal budget consumed by the agent.

Hand-designed reference configurations

Our EQA agent composes navigation, visual inspection, object search, place memory, and answer-generation tools. We first construct two hand-designed configurations as reference points. The quality configuration prioritizes collecting sufficient evidence to answer correctly and receives no explicit instruction to minimize exploration. The efficient configuration is prompted to treat exploration steps as a limited resource and gather evidence more selectively. On HM-EQA, we give the efficient agent a target budget equal to 30% of the nominal allowance, while retaining the same simulator hard limit for both configurations. These configurations provide manually designed operating points for accuracy and efficiency rather than a controlled ablation of a single component.

Workspace-evolution protocol

We next study whether the agent can improve this tradeoff by revising its workspace. We construct fixed evolution pools containing 398 HM-EQA questions and 1,183 MT-HM3D questions from training scenes. During each pass, sixteen workers sample 50 questions from each benchmark, execute them using private workspaces, and reflect on their outcomes. A separate improver aggregates their traces and edits to update the canonical workspace, while all model weights remain fixed. Questions not sampled by the workers are used for monitoring, and their aggregate results are also provided to the improver.

Workspace evolution improves the tradeoff between cost and accuracy

With workspace frozen, pass 17 achieves the highest HM-EQA accuracy (81.2%), while pass 4 performs best on MT-HM3D (66.5%) (Table 5). At low reasoning effort, evolved workspaces use steps comparable to the hand-designed efficient configuration while achieving higher accuracy (Table 4). Improvements vary across revisions as the workspace adds new routines and refines existing guidance. These revisions produce different tradeoffs between accuracy and exploration efficiency.

Learned navigation reduces exploration

In a paired ablation on 132 MT-HM3D questions, ASENA-VLN reduces median normalized exploration steps by approximately 19% with little change in accuracy. Consistent with our previous R2R and RxR results, learned navigation improves efficiency by reducing repeated agent interaction.

4.6 Real-World Applications

We present four demonstrations of ASENA on a Unitree G1 (Fig. 5). All four operate without pre-built maps and combine navigation with search, user interaction, or object delivery. The agent gathers visual and geometric evidence and maintains spatial memory. It writes or revises programs that connect perception and planning with physical actions (Fig. ASENA: Self-evolving Agents for Embodied Navigation).

The three search missions (Fig. 5A–C) take place in previously unseen environments. Search targets are initially outside the robot’s view. In the restroom mission, the robot locates doors near the elevator lobby. It uses its online map to identify a shorter route from the user and returns with directions. In the pantry mission, it locates the room, inspects a dispenser and brewer, and reports two coffee machines. In the snack-comparison mission, it inspects a reference snack and finds a vending machine. It checks whether the same item is available, then returns to answer the user with a generated whole-body gesture. These tasks combine online search and spatial reasoning with evidence collection, memory, and multimodal communication.

The fetch-and-handoff task (Fig. 5D) demonstrates humanoid mobile manipulation by combining navigation, object pickup, carrying while walking, and handoff. After reaching the pantry, the agent uses a head-camera observation to locate the can and ground a grasp. It inspects an arm-motion plan, then uses a YAM gripper to pick up the can. The robot walks back while carrying it. A separately programmed handoff uses inverse kinematics to position it above the recipient’s hand before releasing the gripper. This qualitative demonstration combines navigation, grasp planning, and arm control through the same programming interface.

5 Discussion and Conclusion

ASENA unifies coding-agent programming, robot execution, and persistent skills. It improves recurring-task performance while model weights remain fixed. Our optional 4B monocular ASENA-VLN policy, trained on curated atomic-navigation data, achieves leading R2R/RxR success rates with fewer agent interactions. ASENA also achieves leading EQA accuracy. On G1, online programming extends navigation to search, inspection, and interaction. The agent synthesizes whole-body responses online.

Several limitations remain. The G1 demonstrations provide qualitative evidence of capability composition rather than a systematic measure of reliability across objects, layouts, and users. Real-world tasks take 10–20 minutes, making faster reasoning and execution important for practical use. Future work should evaluate retained skills on new tasks, measure navigation and manipulation reliability over repeated real-world trials, and strengthen safeguards for dynamic environments. Another direction is to extend workspace evolution to both learned policy and agent updates.

Appendix A Supplementary Material

A.1 Atomic Instruction Format and Training Data

Training Sampling

Training uses 64 devices and an effective batch size of 512. Each device processes three trajectory examples and one VQA example per step. We accumulate gradients over two steps. The reported checkpoint uses fewer than 10K optimizer steps and fewer than 5M training samples, including repeats. To emphasize stopping behavior, we add five extra copies of each eligible trajectory-ending window. The pools also include alternative views, CoT variants, and repeated observations.

A.2 Jetson Thor Quantization and Runtime

To run the policy on the G1’s Jetson AGX Thor, we apply post-training FP8 quantization with NVIDIA ModelOpt. We build inference engines with TensorRT-Edge-LLM. These measurements use an earlier ASENA-VLN checkpoint at step 8,400, separate from the benchmark policy in Table 1. Every FP8 variant quantizes the language model. Variants labeled “BF16 vision” keep the 415M-parameter vision encoder in BF16. We leave the embedding and output projection unquantized in all variants.

Navigation-only engines need to predict motion tokens rather than general text. We therefore reduce the output vocabulary from 152,596 to 768 entries while retaining all 660 trajectory tokens. This removes 388.7M parameters from the output projection evaluated at each decoding step.

Measurement protocol

All variants use batch size 1, the same eight-frame mixed-resolution history, and 32 greedy decoding steps. BF16 values are warm medians of five runs. Prefill is time to first token minus visual encoding. Decode scales the remaining 31 tokens to 32 steps. TensorRT-Edge-LLM visual and prefill values are 10-run means. Decode is the median of five runs.

Measured BF16 end-to-end latency is 2,735 ms. The BF16 model occupies 8.28 GiB of allocated memory after loading. This is not a peak runtime measurement.

Table 8 reports latency for each inference component. FP8 with the reduced vocabulary lowers the sum of component latencies from 2,806 to 877 ms, a 3.20×\times speedup over PyTorch BF16 under the same input settings. Decoding remains the largest cost at 683.4 ms, or 78% of the FP8 total. Among the BF16-vision variants, reducing the vocabulary cuts decoding latency from 847.4 to 694.1 ms (18.1%). Visual encoding and prefill latencies stay nearly unchanged.

Table 9 compares quantized and BF16 predictions on held-out inputs. Keeping the vision encoder in BF16 improves agreement for both the first waypoint and the full trajectory. These checks measure output consistency. Navigation success requires separate rollout evaluation. On-device checks also confirmed valid navigation-token IDs and correctly formatted eight-waypoint trajectories.

A.3 Atomic Navigation Dataset Samples

A.4 Navigation Instructions and Policy Inputs

Table 10 shows the navigation instruction format that the policy receives. Each input contains the goal text and a quality setting. An optional end-pose anchor describes where the robot should finish relative to an object, a room, or its starting position.

Directions, route cues, and constraints stay in the instruction text. We express end-pose distances in meters and round them to two decimal places. A room goal uses the relation inside with distance 0.0. All five examples use quality 5. The policy receives this instruction input together with its visual history.

A.5 G1 Hardware and Navigation Settings

The G1 carries a mast-mounted panoramic camera and an inverted Livox Mid-360 LiDAR (Figure 7). A Jetson AGX Thor runs the local sensor and motion services. The camera interface supports both the Insta360 X5 and Ricoh Theta X. Camera yaw correction sets the panorama’s horizontal orientation. The robot’s head and body partially occlude the inverted LiDAR’s view. For manipulation, the G1 uses a calibrated head OAK RGB/stereo camera and optional YAM grippers with fin-ray fingers. Gripper control runs separately from SONIC body motion. Table 11 lists the sensor and state outputs.

Table 12 summarizes the navigation settings and command limits. The slow-walk settings control motion speed, stopping tolerances, command size, and timeouts. They can be adjusted at runtime. A separate walking gait is also available.
